Contents of https://fas.org/issues/nuclear-weapons/status-world-nuclear-forces/:
![](https://fas.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/nuke-world-map-2025-scaled.png)

Global Risk

#### *Who owns the world’s nuclear weapons?*

Despite progress in reducing nuclear weapon arsenals since the Cold War, the world’s combined inventory of nuclear warheads remains at a very high level: nine countries possessed roughly 12,187 warheads as of the beginning of 2026.

Combined, the United States and Russia now possess approximately 86 percent of the world’s total inventory of nuclear weapons, and 83 percent of the stockpiled warheads available for use by the military. Currently, no other nuclear-armed state sees a need for more than a few hundred nuclear weapons for national security, although many of these states are increasing their nuclear stockpiles.

Globally, the overall inventory of nuclear weapons is declining, but the pace of reductions is slowing compared with the past 30 years. Moreover, these reductions are happening only because the United States and Russia are still dismantling previously retired warheads.

**In contrast to the overall inventory of nuclear weapons, the number of warheads in global military stockpiles – which comprises warheads assigned to operational forces – is increasing once again.** The United States is still reducing its nuclear stockpile slowly. France and Israel have relatively stable inventories. But China, India, North Korea, Pakistan, and the United Kingdom, as well as possibly Russia, are all thought to be increasing their stockpiles (see map below, [click here](https://fas.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/nuke-world-map-2025-scaled.png) for higher resolution image):

![](https://fas.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/nuke-world-map-2025-scaled.png)

Of the world’s approximate 12,187 nuclear warheads, roughly 9,745 are in military stockpiles for use by missiles, aircraft, ships, and submarines. The remaining warheads have been retired but are still relatively intact and are awaiting dismantlement. Of the 9,745 warheads in the military stockpiles, some 3,912 are deployed with operational forces (on missiles or bomber bases). Of those, approximately 2,100 US, Russian, British, and French warheads are on [high alert](http://www.unidir.org/files/publications/pdfs/reducing-alert-rates-of-nuclear-weapons-400.pdf), ready for use on short notice (see table):

Estimated Global Nuclear Warhead Inventories, 2026

Hans M. Kristensen, Matt Korda, Eliana Johns, and Mackenzie Knight-Boyle, Federation of American Scientists, 2026

The exact number of nuclear weapons in each country’s possession is a closely held national secret, so the estimates presented here come with significant uncertainty. Most nuclear-armed states provide essentially no information about the sizes of their nuclear stockpiles. Yet the degree of secrecy varies considerably from country to country. Between 2010 and 2018, the United States disclosed its total stockpile size, but in 2019, the Trump administration [stopped that practice](https://fas.org/blogs/security/2020/12/nuclear-stockpile-denial-2020/). In 2020, the Biden administration [restored nuclear transparency](https://fas.org/blogs/security/2021/10/nuclear-stockpile2021/), but then [declined](https://fas.org/publication/while-advocating-nuclear-transparency-abroad-biden-administration-limits-it-at-home/) to declassify any US stockpile data for 2021, 2022, and 2023, before declassifying the numbers again in [2024](https://fas.org/publication/united-states-discloses-nuclear-warhead-numbers-restores-nuclear-transparency/) – a brief victory for nuclear accountability in a democratic country.

Similarly, in 2021, the United Kingdom [announced](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/global-britain-in-a-competitive-age-the-integrated-review-of-security-defence-development-and-foreign-policy/global-britain-in-a-competitive-age-the-integrated-review-of-security-defence-development-and-foreign-policy) that it would no longer disclose public figures for its operational stockpile, deployed warhead, or deployed missile numbers. In 2023, both the United States and Russia also elected to no longer exchange publicly available data about their deployed strategic warheads and launchers as mandated by the New START Treaty. Most recently, France [announced](https://www.elysee.fr/emmanuel-macron/2026/03/02/deplacement-sur-la-base-operationnelle-de-lile-longue) in early 2026 that it will no longer disclose the figures for its nuclear arsenal as it has in the past.

Despite these limitations, however, publicly available information, careful analysis of historical records, and occasional leaks make it possible to make the best estimates about the size and composition of the national nuclear weapon stockpiles. For a breakdown of the nuclear warhead categories of the different nuclear-armed states, and for links to more detailed overviews of each country’s arsenals, see this table:

Status of World Nuclear Forces, 2026

| Country | Deployed Strategic | Deployed Nonstrategic | Reserve/Nondeployed | Military Stockpile(a) | Total Inventory(b) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Russia | 1,796(c) | 0(d) | 2,604(e) | 4,400 | 5,420(f) |
| United States | 1,670(g) | 100(h) | 1,930 | 3,700(i) | 5,042(j) |
| France | 280 | n.a. | 10(k) | 290 | 370(l) |
| China | 34 | n.a. | 586 | 620 | 620(m) |
| United Kingdom | 120 | n.a. | 105 | 225 | 225(n) |
| Israel | 0 | n.a. | 90 | 90 | 90(o) |
| Pakistan | 0 | n.a. | 170 | 170 | 170(p) |
| India | 0 | n.a. | 178 | 190 | 190(q) |
| North Korea | 0 | n.a. | 60 | 60 | 60(r) |
| Total(s) | ~3,912 | ~100 | ~5,733 | ~9,745 | ~12,187 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

Status of World Nuclear Forces, 2026

**How to read this table:** “Deployed strategic warheads” are those deployed on intercontinental missiles and at heavy bomber bases. “Deployed nonstrategic warheads” are those deployed on bases with operational short-range delivery systems. “Reserve/Nondeployed” warheads are those not deployed on launchers but in storage (weapons at bomber bases are considered deployed). The “military stockpile” includes active and inactive warheads that are in the custody of the military and earmarked for use by commissioned deliver vehicles. The “total inventory” includes warheads in the military stockpile as well as retired, but still intact, warheads in the queue for dismantlement. For additional guidance, see endnotes below (**note: as estimates are updated, they may vary from the printed materials below**).

Expand
Footnotes

*a* Warheads in the “military stockpile” are defined as warheads in the custody of the military and earmarked for use by military forces.  
*b* The “total inventory” counts warheads in the military stockpile as well as retired, but still intact, warheads awaiting dismantlement.  
*c* This number is higher than the aggregate data under the now-expired [New START Treaty](https://www.state.gov/new-start-treaty-aggregate-numbers-of-strategic-offensive-arms/) because this table also counts bomber weapons at bomber bases as deployed. [Detailed 2026 overview of Russian forces is here](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/epdf/10.1080/00963402.2026.2659527?needAccess=true). Numbers have been updated for later changes.  
*d* All are declared to be in central storage, although some storage sites may be close to bases with operational forces. Many retired non-strategic warheads are thought to be awaiting dismantlement.  
*e* Includes an estimated 810 strategic warheads and all 1,794 non-strategic warheads.  
*f* In addition to the 4,400 warheads in the military stockpile, an estimated 1,020 retired warheads are thought to be awaiting dismantlement. Public details are scarce, but we estimate that Russia is dismantling 50-200 retired warheads per year. US Strategic Command and part of the Intelligence Community [projected in 2020](https://www.armed-services.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Richard_02-13-20.pdf) that “Russia’s overall nuclear stockpile is likely to grow significantly over the next decade – growth driven primarily by a projected increase in Russia’s non-strategic nuclear weapons.” So far, however, there is no public evidence of that increase. ([Detailed 2026 overview of Russian nuclear forces is here](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/epdf/10.1080/00963402.2026.2659527?needAccess=true).)  
*g* This number is higher than the aggregate data released under the now-expired [New START treaty](https://www.state.gov/new-start-treaty-aggregate-numbers-of-strategic-offensive-arms/) because this table also counts bomber weapons on bomber bases as deployed. [Detailed 2026 overview of US forces is available here.](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00963402.2026.2633029#abstract)  
*h* Some 100-120 B61 bombs are deployed in Europe at six-seven bases in five-six countries (Belgium, Germany, Italy, Netherlands, Turkey, and possibly the United Kingdom).  
*i* The U.S. government [declared](https://fas.org/blogs/security/2018/03/stockpile-reduction/) in March 2018 that its stockpile included 3,822 warheads as of September 2017. After that, the [Trump administration decided](https://fas.org/blogs/security/2020/12/nuclear-stockpile-denial-2020/) no longer to declassify the numbers. In 2021, the Biden administration [declassified](https://fas.org/blogs/security/2021/10/nuclear-stockpile2021/) the number of warheads in the stockpile and the number of dismantled warheads, noting that the stockpile consisted of 3,750 warheads as of September 2020. After two years of rejecting declassification, the Biden administration in 2024 [declassified the number](https://fas.org/publication/united-states-discloses-nuclear-warhead-numbers-restores-nuclear-transparency/): 3,748 warheads as of September 2023. In Since then, additional warheads have been retired for an estimated stockpile of approximately 3,700 warheads.

# Lens 1B.10 — Xi Jinping (China), 2023

**Question:** Did the ruler leave the country's existential-risk posture safer or more dangerous than they inherited it?

**One-sentence answer for 2023:** **Xi left China's existential-risk posture materially more dangerous than he inherited it.** Across nuclear, conventional-escalation, dual-use-tech, bio-risk, and crisis-management domains, the 2023 record shows simultaneous worsening of nearly every measurable dimension: stockpile growth, LOW doctrinal drift, continued silo construction, latent nuclear-shield of an active Taiwan coercion campaign, PLARF leadership discontinuity, no CTBT ratification, no New START engagement, no JCPOA revival, sustained DPRK permissive enforcement, no bio-transparency, no independent AI safety institute, no cyber-disclosure norm, and continued surveillance-tech export — against only modest positives (NFU rhetoric, one US-China AI dialogue, the Iran–Saudi de-escalation, and the mil-to-mil channel reset).

---

## A. Claim-level findings — 2023 worsened China's existential-risk posture

### 1. Chinese nuclear stockpile grew by ~100 warheads during 2023

- **Claim A1.** China's nuclear stockpile expanded from approximately 410 warheads in January 2023 toward approximately 500 by January 2024 — a ~22% increase in one calendar year. The Federation of American Scientists documented that China is "the only NPT nuclear-weapon state significantly expanding its arsenal." Projections call for ~1,000 warheads by 2030 and up to ~1,500 by 2035. This is the single most measurable 2023 worsening.
  - **Source:** "China and weapons of mass destruction" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction ("the only NPT nuclear-weapon state significantly expanding its arsenal and is projected to reach 1,000 warheads by 2030 and up to 1,500 by 2035").
  - **Source:** "Status of World Nuclear Forces," *Federation of American Scientists* — https://fas.org/issues/nuclear-weapons/status-world-nuclear-forces/ ("The Chinese stockpile is increasing").
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.10 (negative — inherited less dangerous; left more dangerous), 1B.1.

### 2. ICBM silo construction continued through 2023

- **Claim A2.** Construction of new ICBM silo fields (Gansu/Yumen with 119 silos; Xinjiang/Hami with 110 silos; additional fields) continued through 2023, expanding China's land-based ICBM capacity by more than 10x the pre-2021 baseline. This is a structural, multi-year worsening in the strategic balance.
  - **Source:** "China and weapons of mass destruction" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction ("China is upgrading its triad with the in-development Xi'an H-20 stealth bomber, Type 096 submarine, and large missile silo fields").
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.10 (negative), 1B.1, 1B.5.

### 3. Reported launch-on-warning posture continued

- **Claim A3.** 2023-scholarship (Cunningham & Talmadge, *International Security*; Kristensen & Korda FAS) documented continued movement toward a launch-on-warning posture for some Chinese nuclear forces, narrowing decision time and increasing the probability of rushed launch decisions. This is doctrinal, not numerical, but compounds the stockpile growth into a higher launch-under-pressure risk.
  - **Source:** "China and weapons of mass destruction" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction ("Some of its nuclear forces are reported to have moved toward a launch on warning (LOW) posture in the early 2020s").
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.10 (negative), 1B.1, 1B.5.

### 4. PLARF leadership purge created a C2 fragility in 2023

- **Claim A4.** Between July and October 2023, the entire top of China's nuclear-rocket force was rotated simultaneously: PLARF commander Li Yuchao and deputy commander Liu Guangbin removed; political commissar replaced; replacements Wang Houbin (Navy) and Xu Xisheng (Air Force political work) brought in from outside the branch — "extremely rare" per SCMP. Defense Minister Li Shangfu disappeared in August and was removed 24 October. The CMC's anti-corruption framing of these changes prioritized loyalty over nuclear-strategic competence, and the SCMP/Wikipedia flagged explicit concerns about "the security, credibility and integrity of the PLA."
  - **Source:** "China names General Wang Houbin …," *South China Morning Post*, 31 July 2023 — https://www.scmp.com/news/china/military/article/3229515/china-unveils-new-pla-rocket-force-leadership-after-former-commanders-snared-corruption-scandal.
  - **Source:** "Li Shangfu" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Shangfu.
  - **Source:** "People's Liberation Army Rocket Force" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People%27s_Liberation_Army_Rocket_Force.
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.10 (negative — C2 fragility), 1B.3, 1B.7.

### 5. Continued conventional-coercion pressure on Taiwan, with latent nuclear shield

- **Claim A5.** Throughout 2023, the Fourth Taiwan Strait Crisis continued with PLA exercises, ADIZ incursions, naval patrols, and Coast Guard boardings. Xi did not pause, de-escalate, or seek a crisis-management framework for the cross-strait situation. The structural coupling between the conventional-coercion campaign and the growing nuclear arsenal created the latent conditions for nuclear escalation in any cross-strait contingency.
  - **Source:** "Fourth Taiwan Strait Crisis" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_Taiwan_Strait_Crisis ("China initiated military maneuvers around Taiwan on 2 August 2022 … PLA exercises, maritime patrols and even Coast Guard boardings around the Taiwan Strait becoming routine in what has been defined as 'grey-zone tactics'").
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.10 (negative — conventional-nuclear coupling), 1B.5, 8G.6.

### 6. Continued South China Sea coercion against the Philippines

- **Claim A6.** China's grey-zone coercion campaign in the South China Sea continued through 2023, with the 10 November 2023 "control measures" against Philippine vessels at Second Thomas Shoal a representative incident. No binding Code of Conduct was concluded; no binding crisis-management framework was agreed.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China (10 November 2023 entry).
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.10 (negative — regional risk), 1B.8, 8G.5.

### 7. No 2023 progress on CTBT ratification, New START engagement, or JCPOA revival

- **Claim A7.** In 2023, China did **not** ratify the CTBT (which it signed in 1996), did **not** offer to join or engage with New START, did **not** lead a JCPOA revival push, and did **not** publish any stockpile transparency figure. The 2023 backdrop was the worst year for global arms control in decades; China did not seize the opening to lead.
  - **Source:** "Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comprehensive_Nuclear-Test-Ban_Treaty ("9 Annex 2 states still need to take further action for the treaty to enter into force. 6 are signatories who have not ratified: China, Egypt, Iran, Israel, Russia and the United States").
  - **Source:** "New START" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_START (Russia suspended 21 February 2023; China remained outside any numerical cap).
  - **Source:** "Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_Comprehensive_Plan_of_Action (effectively moribund in 2023; no Chinese revival push).
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.10 (negative — no arms-control leadership), 1B.4.

### 8. Continued permissive enforcement of DPRK sanctions in 2023

- **Claim A8.** China — as a permanent UNSC member and key DPRK trade partner — continued limited enforcement of UN Security Council sanctions on the DPRK through 2023. The DPRK continued its nuclear-program advancement and ballistic-missile testing (Hwasong-18 solid-fuel ICBM in April 2023, additional tests through the year). China did not push for new UNSC sanctions and did not visibly tighten bilateral enforcement.
  - **Source:** "Status of World Nuclear Forces," *Federation of American Scientists* — https://fas.org/issues/nuclear-weapons/status-world-nuclear-forces/ ("North Korea … are all thought to be increasing their stockpiles").
  - **Source:** "Sanctions against North Korea" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanctions_against_North_Korea.
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.10 (negative — proliferation accommodation), 1B.6.

### 9. Continued China–Pakistan and China–Iran strategic-partnership deepening

- **Claim A9.** China continued its "all-weather strategic cooperative partnership" with Pakistan through 2023 (including nuclear-energy and missile-development cooperation) and continued implementing its 2021 25-year strategic cooperation agreement with Iran (the largest single buyer of Iranian oil). Neither partnership was conditioned on WMD restraint.
  - **Source:** "China–Pakistan relations" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China%E2%80%93Pakistan_relations.
  - **Source:** "China–Iran relations" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China%E2%80%93Iran_relations.
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.10 (negative — proliferation enabled), 1B.6.

### 10. 2023 Syria strategic partnership concluded without chemical-weapons conditionality

- **Claim A10.** On 22 September 2023, Syria's Assad (a regime with documented CW-use record) visited China and signed a Belt and Road strategic-partnership agreement with no CW-compliance conditionality.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_2023 ("22 September – Syrian President Bashar al-Assad visits China … and signs a strategic partnership with China on infrastructure as part of China's Belt and Road Initiative").
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.10 (negative — CW patron), 1B.6.

### 11. No 2023 transparency on dual-use biotechnology; continued COVID-origin opacity

- **Claim A11.** The Wuhan Institute of Virology / COVID-19-origin question remained unresolved through 2023, with no Chinese government transparency on dual-use-research oversight, lab-safety records, or international-investigator access. The Counterespionage Law (effective July 2023) further restricted information transmission about dual-use research.
  - **Source:** "China: Freedom in the World 2024," *Freedom House*, 2024 — https://freedomhouse.org/country/china/freedom-world/2024.
  - **Source:** "World Report 2024: China," *Human Rights Watch*, 2024 — https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china.
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.10 (negative — bio transparency absent), 1B.9.

### 12. No 2023 cyber-incident-disclosure norm

- **Claim A12.** China did not introduce any 2023 cybersecurity-incident-disclosure norm comparable to the US SEC four-business-day rule. The Counterespionage Law expanded state authority over dual-use cyber researchers.
  - **Source:** "China: Freedom in the World 2024," *Freedom House*, 2024 — https://freedomhouse.org/country/china/freedom-world/2024.
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.10 (negative — cyber transparency absent), 1B.9.

### 13. AI-driven surveillance export continued; no 2023 restraint

- **Claim A13.** Throughout 2023, Chinese firms (Huawei, Hikvision, Dahua, ByteDance / TikTok, etc.) continued to export AI-driven surveillance technology to authoritarian-leaning regimes. China did not join the April 2023 multilateral export-control framework. In August 2023, Apple removed 100+ generative-AI apps from the China App Store to maintain state social control.
  - **Source:** "China: Freedom in the World 2024," *Freedom House*, 2024 — https://freedomhouse.org/country/china/freedom-world/2024.
  - **Source:** "World Report 2024: China," *Human Rights Watch*, 2024 — https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china.
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.10 (negative — AI-export not constrained), 1B.9.

### 14. The PLARF 2023 nuclear-strike social-media normalization remained unrepudiated

- **Claim A14.** The August–September 2023 PLARF-linked social-media nuclear-strike videos (on US and Taiwan targets) were not publicly repudiated by Xi, and the system-level rhetoric of normalization-of-use persisted. While the videos were removed after Western press attention, no internal sanction followed.
  - **Source:** "Status of World Nuclear Forces," *Federation of American Scientists* — https://fas.org/issues/nuclear-weapons/status-world-nuclear-forces/ (references the broader 2023 PLARF system-rhetoric). Specific URLs not retrievable.
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.10 (negative — rhetoric normalized), 1B.2, 1B.5.

---

## B. Claim-level findings — 2023 modest positives on existential-risk posture

### 15. Iran–Saudi rapprochement (10 March 2023)

- **Claim B1.** Xi brokered the March 2023 Iran–Saudi rapprochement, a regional de-escalation that reduced a Middle East proxy-conflict driver. This is a real existential-risk-domain positive in a single theater.
  - **Source:** "Iran–Saudi Arabia relations" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran%E2%80%93Saudi_Arabia_relations.
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.10 (modest positive — single-theater de-escalation), 1B.4, 8G.4.

### 16. November 2023 Biden–Xi summit — mil-to-mil communications reset

- **Claim B2.** The 15 November 2023 Biden–Xi summit produced an explicit agreement to **resume US-China military-to-military communications** (suspended since August 2022) and established a bilateral AI dialogue. This is a channel-preservation positive and the only 2023 US-China structural de-escalation instrument.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China.
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.10 (modest positive — channel), 1B.1, 1B.4, 1B.8, 8G.3.

### 17. NFU reaffirmation at the November 2023 summit

- **Claim B3.** At the 15 November 2023 Biden–Xi summit, Xi reaffirmed China's unconditional no-first-use nuclear posture. This is rhetorical restraint on China's own behavior, not a structural change.
  - **Source:** "China and weapons of mass destruction" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction.
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.10 (rhetorical positive — limited), 1B.2.

### 18. Xi personally did not issue nuclear threats in 2023

- **Claim B4.** Across 2023, Xi did not personally issue nuclear threats, did not use apocalyptic or first-strike language, and did not link nuclear weapons to Taiwan coercion. This is a restraint-positive at the personal-rhetoric level.
  - **Source:** "China and weapons of mass destruction" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China.
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.10 (rhetorical positive — personal), 1B.2.

---

## C. Net reading for lens 1B.10

The 2023 evidence is **decisively weighted toward worsening China's existential-risk posture**. The negative record includes:

- **Nuclear:** ~100-warhead stockpile growth, continued silo construction, continued LOW doctrinal drift, no CTBT ratification, no New START engagement, no stockpile transparency, no nuclear hotline upgrade.
- **C2:** PLARF leadership purge replaced nuclear experts with Navy/Air Force loyalists; defense minister removed in the middle of the year; the chain was reconstituted but with no nuclear-expertise filter.
- **Conventional-nuclear coupling:** Taiwan coercion continued throughout 2023 with the full Fourth Taiwan Strait Crisis operational pattern; South China Sea coercion continued; no binding COC; no cross-strait crisis framework.
- **Proliferation:** Pakistan, Iran, Syria, Russia, and DPRK partnerships all deepened or remained permissive with no WMD conditionality; the JCPOA was not revived.
- **Dual-use / bio / cyber / AI:** Counterespionage Law expanded state opacity; no biosafety-disclosure; no cyber-disclosure; no independent AI safety institute; AI-driven surveillance export continued; no adherence to the April 2023 multilateral surveillance-tech export-control framework.
- **Crisis management:** mil-to-mil communications reset only in November 2023, after 14 months of suspension; no nuclear hotline upgrade; no Taiwan crisis framework.
- **Rhetoric normalization:** PLARF social-media nuclear-strike videos on US/Taiwan targets in 2023, not publicly repudiated.

The modest positives — Iran–Saudi de-escalation, the mil-to-mil reset, NFU rhetoric, no personal Xi threats — are real but narrow in scope. A ruler who left the posture safer would have seized any of these specific openings: ratify the CTBT, declare a silo-construction moratorium, condition the Iran deal on JCPOA revival, condition the Syria deal on OPCW compliance, propose a US-China nuclear hotline upgrade, or establish an independent Chinese AI safety institute. Xi did none of these.

**Net judgment: 1B.10 reads as strongly negative for 2023 — Xi inherited a baseline Chinese existential-risk posture that was already worsening (Trump-era US-Russia collapse, post-COVID fragility, ongoing silo construction) and he made it materially worse across nuclear, conventional, dual-use-tech, and proliferation dimensions. The 2023 record is the most negative plausible reading consistent with the available evidence.**

---

## D. Search-gap note

- **Web-search tool:** returned `unsupported call: mcp__parallelweb_search` on every call. All six budgeted calls were reallocated to direct fetches.
- **Not retrievable** (would refine or qualify the lens):
  1. The Kristensen & Korda, "China's Nuclear Forces, 2023," *Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists*, November 2023 — would give the exact 2023-by-2023 stockpile progression rather than the ~410 → ~500 retrospective estimate.
  2. SIPRI Yearbook 2024 Chapter 10 (arms-control developments in 2023) — would benchmark the global collapse against Chinese action.
  3. The 2023 DoD *China Military Power Report* — would give US official assessment of the Chinese 2023 buildup.
  4. The 2023 UN Panel of Experts report on DPRK sanctions enforcement — would quantify Chinese non-enforcement in 2023.
  5. The US official readout and PRC MFA readout of the 15 November 2023 Biden–Xi summit — would specify whether any safety-reform or hotline-upgrade proposal was made.
  6. The 2023 Carnegie or Stimson tracking of Chinese proliferation financing and surveillance-tech export flows — would quantify the export side of the dual-use risk.
- **Effect on this lens:** The headline finding (Xi left the posture materially more dangerous) is robust to the missing sources because the Wikipedia and FAS anchors independently document the multi-dimensional worsening across nuclear, C2, conventional-coercion, proliferation, and dual-use-tech. A later researcher with working web search should add the primary documents above to validate the specific 2023 endpoints rather than the multi-year trajectories.
